title: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
desc: Treats production, training, selection and profit sharing as interdependent, with unequal development access and weak long-term incentives.

kps.k: The cluster treats law-firm structure as an interdependent system of production, training, promotion and profit sharing—not simply a staffing pyramid.
kps.d: Galanter and Palay’s 1991 tournament model explains how partners exchange reputation, clients and expertise for associates’ labour, using prospective partnership as deferred compensation and a constraint on opportunism. Promoting successive cohorts then generates demand for more associates and continued growth. Gilson and Mnookin’s 1985 account adds a different rationale: sharing income diversifies lawyers’ career risks, provided firms constrain shirking, demands for larger shares and departures. Historical accounts explain the Cravath system’s success through expanding corporate demand, graduate supply, durable client relationships and limited mobility rather than inherent organizational superiority. The supplied account of the 1991 book is a reconstruction, not access to its full empirical analyses; it also distinguishes tournament incentives from mandatory dismissal of unsuccessful candidates.

qs.q: Specifically, by observing the treatment of preceding classes, an associate could verify that the firm was making good on its commitment.53     As noted in Tournament of Lawyers, because each newly promoted partner requires the hiring of additional associates, the maintenance of the tournament essentially commits the firm to a long-term pattern of perpetual growth.
qs.a: The Elastic Tournament: A Second Transformation of the Big Law Firm · Academia · 2008

qs.q: We conclude that, contrary to the new conventional wisdom, because sharing facilitates diversification, the sharing model is superior, provided that shirking, grabbing, and leaving can be constrained.
qs.a: Sharing Among the Human Capitalists: An Economic Inquiry into the Corporate Law Firm and How Partners Split Profits · Academia · 1985

kps.k: The revised tournament explains unequal access to development and forward-looking selection rather than an equal contest rewarding past performance.
kps.d: Wilkins and Gulati’s 1996 and 1998 analyses distinguish routine production from assignments that develop expertise, client contact and sponsorship. Partners ration costly training toward their own practices and protégés; prestigious credentials can secure early opportunities partly because they signal firm quality, not because they reliably predict legal ability. These advantages accumulate, although associates can change tracks. Partnership decisions depend on expected future revenue, relationships and business demand, leaving associates exposed to market fluctuations. Wages, transferable training and employment reputation also motivate juniors who never seek partnership: only 33 of 183 respondents in their informal poll reported joining with that intention. The account draws on interviews, published research and informal polling rather than a comprehensive causal test.

qs.q: Associates who are being trained are also likely to be monitored.” More important, the training track provides the gate- way to the real promotion-to-partner tournament, since only those associates who have been trained will have the firm-specific and relational capital that it takes to have a realistic chance of becom- ing partners in the firm.
qs.a: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms · Academia · 1998

qs.q: In Part II, however, we demonstrated that firms make partner- ship decisions not as a reward for past associate performance, but as a prediction of which partner candidates will contribute the most in the future.
qs.a: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms · Academia · 1998

kps.k: Partnership increasingly extends competition rather than ending it.
kps.d: Galanter and Henderson’s 2008 elastic tournament describes an ownership core surrounded by permanent associates, counsel, non-equity partners and other employees. Equity partners themselves face differentiated compensation, de-equitization and forced departure. They report that NLJ 250 firms disclosing at least one non-equity partner increased from 42.4% in 1993 to 74.8% in 2007, with incomplete disclosure potentially understating the change. From Big Law to Lean Law reports a further staffing divergence in 2010–2011: NLJ 250 headcount grew 1.7%, associate numbers fell 1.3%, and other-attorney numbers rose 17.2%. These observations support differentiation of careers, not a uniform trajectory across firms or proof that additional tiers improve long-term performance.

qs.q: Between 2010 and 2011, the total lawyer headcount for firms in the NLJ 250 (a ranking of total number of lawyers for U.S.-based law firms) increased from 124,161 to 126,293, which reflected an overall growth rate of 1.7%.
qs.a: From Big Law to Lean Law · Academia · 2014

qs.q: 43 Yet, total associate headcount dropped 1.3% (from 60,377 to 59,574) while the “other” attorney category grew an astounding 17.2% (from 11,376 to 13,332).
qs.a: From Big Law to Lean Law · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Client sophistication and lawyer mobility jointly reshape firms, but institutional relationships remain important.
kps.d: The client-led ecosystem accounts argue that stronger in-house departments insource work, scrutinize fees and staffing, and recruit experienced firm lawyers. Portable client relationships strengthen rainmakers’ bargaining power and encourage revenue-based compensation. Getting In and Out of the House explicitly rejects attributing restructuring solely to client pressure: partners’ demands, interfirm competition and management choices also matter. Team of Rivals qualifies claims that clients simply hire individuals rather than firms. Nearly 80% of surveyed general counsel reported terminating important firm relationships no more than twice during 2003–2006. Wilkins interprets persistence through switching costs, team knowledge and interdependence—not necessarily satisfaction. Mobility can therefore destabilize internal labour markets without eliminating firm-level value.

qs.q: Rather, some of these measures were adopted in response to demands by rainmaking partners to abandon lockstep arrangements and to increase their compensation, all in the context of increased mobility and the implied threat that failure to yield may cause them to leave.
qs.a: Getting In and Out of the House: The Worlds of In-House Counsel, Big Law, and Emerging Career Trajectories of In-House Lawyers · Academia · 2020

qs.q: Nearly 80% of the general counsel in our sample claimed that at most they had terminated an important law firm relationship "once or twice" between 2003 and 2006, with almost a third (31%) conceding that they had never done so during the period.
qs.a: Team of Rivals? Toward a New Model of the Corporate Attorney-Client Relationship · Academia · 2010

kps.k: Current partner profits can coexist with weak incentives to build enduring firm capabilities.
kps.d: Gilson and Mnookin, Ribstein and From Big Law to Lean Law identify a tension between rewarding individual business generation and financing collective reputation, supervision, teamwork and processes. Sharing can support institution-building but becomes difficult when successful partners can depart with clients. A 2012 survey cited in Lean Law found that 74% of respondents rated origination very important to compensation, compared with 9% for management and 10% for good citizenship. Tellmann adds that departing partners’ extinguished equity interests and differing retirement horizons can favour distributions over technology investment. Ribstein also distinguishes distributable profits from risk-adjusted value: additional salaried associates amplify both gains and losses and can strain supervision. These are proposed mechanisms, not proof that every revenue-based compensation system fails.

qs.q: Big Law’s reputational bonding model founders on the problem that compensation based on business generation does not motivate lawyers to devote time to firm- building, and equal or seniority-based compensation that rewards firm- building is difficult to sustain as long as lawyers can leave and take their clients with them.
qs.a: The Death of Big Law · Academia · 2010

qs.q: Figure 4  When asked to assess the importance of various factors that are considered in determining compensation at their firms, origination of business was ranked as the most important factor (74% picking “very important”) followed by revenues generated through that partner’s work for clients (59%).
qs.a: From Big Law to Lean Law · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Apprenticeship faces a financing and coordination problem that predates generative AI.
kps.d: The Leadership Imperative links client resistance to junior charges, expensive talent, early specialization and attrition in a reinforcing cycle: weak development encourages departure, which further reduces incentives to train. Lower associate-to-partner ratios after the financial crisis do not necessarily relieve the problem if partners devote more time to business generation. In-house departments also depend on experienced recruits, making training a shared supply problem rather than solely a firm expense. Evidence remains mixed in form: a study cited in The Elastic Tournament associates developmental work, family-friendly conditions and clearer partnership communication with intentions to stay, while pay has no independent relationship after controls. That finding concerns retention intentions, not demonstrated causal effects. Quantitative Legal Prediction further qualifies departure costs: alumni who become in-house buyers may return business to the firm.

qs.q: The investment can be recaptured if that in-house counsel is persuaded to drive business in the firm’s direction.
qs.a: Quantitative Legal Prediction — or — How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Start Preparing for the Data-Driven Future of the Legal Services Industry · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Unequal development and opaque evaluation challenge meritocratic accounts of law-firm careers.
kps.d: Wilkins and Gulati argue that firms can remain profitable while losing Black talent because routine production and selective training still supply enough successors. Their 1996 preliminary survey reports that 61% of respondents struggled to obtain quality assignments; this supports concern about development but does not establish a definitive causal estimate of discrimination. Their later model explains selective disclosure as an effort and retention mechanism, not an endorsement of concealment. Long-hours and unpredictable-availability norms can separately disadvantage women with family responsibilities. Historical accounts also reject nostalgia for an inclusive Cravath era. The practical implication advanced across these works is that diversity initiatives and formal training policies must address assignment access, sponsorship and partner incentives; courses or moral appeals alone may leave those mechanisms intact.

qs.q: 1996]                WHY ARE THERE SO FEW BLACK LAWYERS  "good for business." So long as firms continue to generate both a small number of high quality partners and a steady supply of hard- working associates, they have little economic reason to alter the way they structure their business simply to change the demographic compo- sition of tournament winners.33
qs.a: Why Are There So Few Black Lawyers in Corporate Law Firms? An Institutional Analysis · Academia · 1996

qs.q: Instead, firms pursue a “black box” approach in which associates are provided only a vague idea about the criteria for making partner and almost no in- formation about how these criteria are applied in particular cases.
qs.a: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms · Academia · 1998

kps.k: The debate remains divided over whether these pressures imply decline, adaptation or persistent instability.
kps.d: Ribstein’s 2010 structural diagnosis predicts a diminished role for large firms and smaller, flatter organizations, while allowing exceptions. His reported 2009 headcount losses establish stress, not the disappearance of Big Law. Lean Law argues that flat demand cannot support perpetual organic growth but allows familiar brands and adapting firms to survive. By contrast, the 2020 Getting In and Out of the House predicts continued expert work and volatility rather than demise. The Transformation of Corporate Legal Practice makes viability conditional on responses to clients, competitors and talent pressures. Even The Elastic Tournament is internally qualified: its abstract calls the model economically stable, while its conclusion leaves stability unresolved. The supplied material does not adjudicate these forecasts with subsequent outcome evidence.

qs.q: The result is likely to be the end of the major role large law firms have played in the delivery of legal services.
qs.a: The Death of Big Law · Academia · 2010

qs.q: The revised account also explains why the relative decline of large law firms’ profitability has not led, and is not likely to lead, to the demise of Big Law.
qs.a: Getting In and Out of the House: The Worlds of In-House Counsel, Big Law, and Emerging Career Trajectories of In-House Lawyers · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Neither promotion tournaments nor associate-heavy pyramids provide a universal explanation of legal organization.
kps.d: Hierarchies, Specialization, and the Utilization of Knowledge reports that 73% of US law offices had no associates in the 1992 Census of Services and 11% had exactly one. These are office-level observations, not firm-level statistics. The authors use specialization patterns to motivate an alternative account in which hierarchy expands the use of expert knowledge; the supplied excerpts do not include the subsequent empirical tests. What Is a Professional Service Firm? reports Morris and Pinnington’s finding that only one-quarter of a broad UK law-firm sample used up-or-out and their interpretation that professional ideology better explained its variation than incentive theories. The Price of Law adds reputation and high-stakes relative performance as pricing mechanisms, but its litigation tournament is distinct from associate promotion. These contributions limit generalization from elite US corporate firms.

qs.q: 73% of law offices have no associates: these “non-hierarchies” include, for example, single-lawyer offices and offices where there are several lawyers, all of whom are partners.
qs.a: Hierarchies, Specialization, and the Utilization of Knowledge: Theory and Evidence from the Legal Services Industry · Academia · 2004

qs.q: Second, they argued that the variation of up-orout across law firms was not consistent with incentive-based theories but, instead, was consistent with variations in the strength of professional ideology: “Patterns of up-or-out usage suggest it exists for reasons other than just to minimize monitoring costs.
qs.a: What Is a Professional Service Firm? Toward a Theory and Taxonomy of Knowledge-Intensive Firms · Academia · 2010

kps.k: Proposed reforms seek to make development and collective investment economically sustainable, with no assured successor model.
kps.d: Wilkins and Gulati propose fairer assignment management, teamwork and non-hourly fees; Galanter and Henderson envisage employee-based firms built around durable processes and profitable matter management. Ribstein favours firm-owned productive assets capable of attracting capital, stressing that permission for outside investment alone cannot repair an aggregation of mobile lawyers. Team of Rivals proposes long-term client partnerships that support junior development but warns of supplier dependence and client-failure exposure. The Leadership Imperative instead emphasizes shared responsibility among schools, firms and corporate clients for transferable skills and networks. Ethical benefits also remain conditional: risk sharing may support independence, but outside-firm status does not itself establish superior gatekeeping. These are reform proposals with implementation constraints, not demonstrated solutions.

qs.q: and hours that is often found in in-house legal departments.263 Promotions would not be based on a multi-year tournament but on a lawyer’s ability to profitably manage client matters, often taken a flat-fee basis or another non- hourly alternative.264 Demonstrated management and teamwork skills resulting in successful client engagements would carry more weight than Ivy-league credentials.
qs.a: The Elastic Tournament: A Second Transformation of the Big Law Firm · Academia · 2008

qs.a: The Death of Big Law · Academia · 2010

kps.k: The AI-era contribution is that technology’s organizational effects depend on inherited incentives, not technical capability alone.
kps.d: How Artificial Intelligence Will Affect the Practice of Law treats client cost pressure as the impetus for restructuring and technology as an enabler that could benefit equity partners. Fighting the Hypothetical predicts that compensation and prestige will shape responses to GenAI; it considers alternative staffing and cites subcontractor markups as a possible replacement for associate-labour margins, leaving profit effects unresolved. Tellmann predicts eventual erosion of hourly billing while acknowledging its continuing centrality. These excerpts provide conceptual extensions of the older institutional debate, not quantified evidence that AI has displaced associates or ended hourly billing. The bibliography-only excerpt from It’s the End of the World as We Know It supplies no substantive AI finding.

qs.q: Technological advances provide the tools for law firms to facilitate this transition, and make it not only financially viable but also potentially lucrative for a firm’s equity partners.
qs.a: How Artificial Intelligence Will Affect the Practice of Law · Academia · 2018

qs.q: Both of those factors are likely to play a major role in response to GenAI’s likely seismic effect on each factor.
qs.a: Fighting the Hypothetical: Why Law Firms Should Rethink the Billable Hour in the Generative AI Era · Academia · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated academia and research sources generally accept the proposition’s core and materially develop it into a broader institutional account. Their common explanation is that production, training, promotion and profit sharing operate together: costly and selectively allocated training shapes who can compete; partnership decisions are forward-looking and depend on sponsorship, client demand and expected business generation; and promotion increasingly leads into further contests over equity status, compensation, clients and continued tenure. Several sources connect this post-partnership competition to lateral mobility, stronger in-house purchasing, revenue-based compensation, de-equitization and weaker incentives to invest in supervision, technology and other firmwide capabilities. They also deepen the proposition by showing that development opportunities are unequal and opaque, with particular implications for Black lawyers, women and other historically excluded groups.

There is material internal variation. Foundational tournament theory originally frames partnership as the associate contest’s prize, whereas later work replaces that terminal model with a multiround or elastic tournament. Some sources support only the wider systemic or historical elements, such as the Cravath model’s contingent alignment with client and labour markets, without directly examining post-partnership competition. Others redirect toward alternative explanations—knowledge utilisation, professional ideology or winner-take-all legal pricing—and caution against generalising from elite US corporate firms to law offices or professional-service firms generally. A few excerpts are too bibliographic or reportorial to establish an authorial position. Reform proposals also differ substantially, ranging from shared responsibility for lawyer development and long-term non-hourly client relationships to employee-based firms, professional assignment management and firm-owned productive assets. These proposals are presented as possible institutional responses, not demonstrated successor models. Overall, the voice builds on the proposition, but this conclusion characterises the supplied selection rather than academia or research as a whole.

qs.q: A growing num- ber of firms have specifically adopted a two-tiered partnership structure in which “junior” (salaried) partners compete to become “senior” (equity) partners.” Unlike the promotion-to-partner tour- nament, the sole criteria for winning this “partner” tournament is a junior partner’s demonstrated ability to bring in business and to as- sume primary responsibility on major matters for senior partners.
qs.a: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms · Academia · 1998

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources collectively build the institutional foundations of the proposition. They treat the law firm as an interdependent system linking production, costly monitoring, selective training, promotion, profit sharing, client purchasing and lawyer mobility. The principal development is from the original, relatively simple promotion tournament—where partnership is the prize—to multiround and “elastic” accounts in which access to developmental work is unequal, promotion is forward-looking, and competition continues among salaried, non-equity and equity partners through business-generation demands, differentiated compensation, de-equitization and lateral exit. Common explanations include the cost of supervising and training juniors, clients’ resistance to paying for junior development, partners’ incentives to ration training toward their own practices, and the tension between rewarding portable client business and investing in collective capabilities. Material internal variation remains. The original Galanter–Palay model partly conflicts with the proposition by treating partnership as the endpoint of associate competition, while later work revises it. Other sources redirect attention toward knowledge utilisation, professional ideology, winner-take-all pricing or the limited applicability of associate-heavy hierarchies; these qualify generalisation beyond elite corporate firms rather than overturning the proposition within its intended domain. Reform proposals also diverge—from long-term non-hourly client alliances and professional assignment management to flatter firms and firm-owned productive assets—and remain proposals rather than demonstrated successor models. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis describes the relationship among these selected sources and does not establish how prevalent any position was in the period.

qs.q: A plausible model of the internal labor markets of elite firms, therefore, must account for the fact that these institutions must re- solve two separate, albeit interrelated, problems: monitoring and training.
qs.a: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms · Academia · 1998

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources accept the proposition’s core claim that law-firm production, training, promotion and profit sharing operate as an interdependent system, and materially develop it for a later period. Their common explanation is that stronger in-house departments, client resistance to funding junior training, lateral mobility and rainmaker bargaining weakened the old alignment of apprenticeship, up-or-out promotion, lockstep compensation and stable partnership. Firms consequently added permanent-associate, counsel and non-equity-partner tiers, lengthened partnership paths, differentiated partner compensation and exposed partners to de-equitization or departure—directly supporting the proposition that partnership extends rather than ends competition. The sources also connect these changes to weaker incentives for broad, long-term associate development and propose shared responsibility among law schools, firms and corporate legal departments. Material variation concerns causation and outlook: some emphasize client-led restructuring, while others insist that partner demands, interfirm competition, management choices and talent markets are also important; forecasts range from continued instability and adaptation to conditional concern about the model’s viability. The AI-focused source adds that technology enables economically driven restructuring rather than independently determining it. These positions characterize only the supplied curated sources, not all commentary from the period.

The curated 2025 sources collectively build on the proposition that law-firm production, training, promotion and profit sharing form an interdependent system in which partnership does not eliminate competitive pressures. Their principal extension is to AI adoption: established compensation metrics, prestige incentives and reliance on associate leverage are presented as mechanisms likely to shape firms’ responses to GenAI, including whether they change staffing or billing models. A complementary historical account explains why these mechanisms are durable, linking apprenticeship to legal production and treating time-based billing as a proxy for value under conditions of trust, reputation and information asymmetry. Material variation remains. “Fighting the Hypothetical” directly predicts substantial GenAI disruption but leaves effects on staffing and profits unresolved; “Opportunities and Challenges in Legal AI” supplies an indirect historical and organisational explanation rather than evidence of adoption at scale; and the bibliography-only excerpt establishes no discernible authorial position. Accordingly, the period extends the cluster’s institutional explanation but does not provide quantified evidence that AI had already transformed staffing, partner competition or billing at scale in 2025.

qs.q: Both of those factors are likely to play a major role in response to GenAI’s likely seismic effect on each factor.
qs.a: Fighting the Hypothetical: Why Law Firms Should Rethink the Billable Hour in the Generative AI Era · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In effect, work product creation in the profession and skill development and training are intimately interrelated.
qs.a: Opportunities and Challenges in Legal AI · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The sole curated 2026 source accepts the proposition’s systemic framing of law-firm production, training and profit sharing and materially develops its account of weak long-term incentives. Tellmann links associate leverage, attrition, partner business-development demands and client resistance to a reinforcing erosion of apprenticeship, rather than treating training failure as an isolated consequence of AI. He further extends the proposition by arguing that mobile partners, extinguished equity interests and divergent retirement horizons can favour current distributions over sustained technology investment. The source is more focused on institutional economics than on the proposition’s claims about unequal development access or competition continuing after promotion to partnership. It also distinguishes present conditions from prediction: hourly billing remains central, while its eventual erosion is forecast rather than demonstrated. With only one curated source in this period, this position should not be read as representative of 2026 commentary generally.

qs.q: If law firm managers are generally in their late-fifties or early-          sixties, one can expect investments designed to generate returns over a          period of several years, but not much longer.502  The result can lead to underinvestment in technology.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026
